{"id": "91:9/q09", "question": "What is the answer to the preceding oath, and what role does this clause play?", "turns_on": "Whether the long oath licenses omission of lām or the whole answer, or syntactic inversion; the Thamūd narrative helps infer an omitted threat.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q09/p1", "position": "This success clause answers the oath, with an understood lām before qad.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl and al-Zajjāj supply la-qad; al-Zajjāj says the long passage compensates for omitted lām. Ibn ʿAbbās counts eleven oaths; al-Rāzī reports seven sworn things. Al-Ṭabarī cites Qatāda. Al-Bayḍāwī says the oaths urge knowledge and gratitude. Al-Ālūsī argues lām omission is common and easier than omitting an entire answer, invokes 23:1, and says purification itself merits emphasis. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 92:4–5."}, {"id": "91:9/q09/p2", "position": "The oath's answer is omitted: God will destroy Meccan deniers as He destroyed Thamūd; this clause is an aside.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī connects this to denial of Muḥammad and Ṣāliḥ and 91:11–14, placing the tangent after 91:8. Al-Nasafī calls it more evident; Qāshānī calls the doomed veiled deniers. Iṣlāḥī says suppression permits all implications of the oaths, prominently destruction of rebellious nations. Al-Ālūsī disputes omission of a whole answer."}, {"id": "91:9/q09/p3", "position": "The omitted oath answer is that the hearers will surely be resurrected.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān report the supplied la-tubʿathunna."}, {"id": "91:9/q09/p4", "position": "The success and failure clauses are placed before the oath by inversion.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Qurṭubī report fronting and postponement rather than an omitted answer."}, {"id": "91:9/q09/p5", "position": "This clause interrupts the oath to explain moral choice, with the oath answer left open.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr allows both oath answer and interruption explaining success by following divinely indicated piety. Iṣlāḥī favors a suppressed complement whose implications include judgment on rebellion."}]}
{"id": "91:9/q10", "question": "What prophetic reports are connected to reciting this verse and asking for purification?", "turns_on": "The setting and wording of the prayer, and the strength of specific routes.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q10/p1", "position": "The Prophet paused at this verse and prayed for his soul's piety and purification.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl transmits the pause and prayer, calling God guardian and best purifier. Ibn Kathīr cites al-Ṭabarānī's Ibn ʿAbbās route and al-Haythamī's ḥasan grading; Abū Hurayra's route is absent from major collectors. Elmalılı and al-Ālūsī also cite Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "91:9/q10/p2", "position": "The Prophet taught or recited a wider prayer asking God to grant the soul piety and purify it.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Arqam's report includes refuge from incapacity, laziness, miserliness, cowardice, senility or worry, grave punishment, useless knowledge, an unsated soul, an unhumble heart, and unanswered prayer. Muslim transmits it; Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Nasāʾī are also cited. ʿĀʾisha reports finding the Prophet praying in prostration; Ibn Kathīr says Aḥmad alone transmits it."}, {"id": "91:9/q10/p3", "position": "A reported prophetic gloss says the soul God purifies succeeds and the one He deprives of good fails.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr questions the route through Juwaybir, abandoned in hadith, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who never met Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ālūsī cites other collections without grading."}]}
{"id": "91:9/q11", "question": "What does the verse teach about human responsibility and divine decree?", "turns_on": "Whether human action is independent, acquired under divine creation, or determined by prior decree.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q11/p1", "position": "People must choose and cultivate good and are responsible for corrupting the soul.", "reasons": "Quṭb describes a conscious discerning faculty; Iṣlāḥī says moral awareness obliges choice and compares neglect to shutting one's eyes near danger. Elmalılı cites 47:7 for striving that brings divine help. Al-Zamakhsharī says inspiration clarifies the difference and enables choice; Ibn Kathīr cites 87:14–15."}, {"id": "91:9/q11/p2", "position": "God creates and enables acts, while human participation warrants attribution and responsibility.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says attribution need not imply independent creation or autonomous choice. Elmalılı distinguishes God's creation and human acquisition; the Study Quran cites 35:18, 76:30, 4:49, 24:21 and 13:11 for will and change. Al-Biqāʿī says God enables each person's created path."}, {"id": "91:9/q11/p3", "position": "God's prior purification or abandonment determines the outcome outside independent human action.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī invokes prior decree; al-Rāzī takes 91:8 as God granting piety or abandoning the wicked; al-Intiṣāf cites divine subjects in preceding oaths. Al-Zamakhsharī rejects attributing evil destiny to God."}]}
{"id": "91:9/q12", "question": "What inward forms of purification or success are drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "Different spiritual practices or states are singled out as the inward realization of success.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q12/p1", "position": "Success is attending carefully to each moment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, reported by al-Sulamī."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p2", "position": "Success is scrutinizing the source of one's food.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān al-Maghribī opposes it to negligence."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p3", "position": "Success is protecting the inner secret from worldly pollution.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir contrasts this with preoccupation with the world."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p4", "position": "Success is knowing what God requires and addresses to oneself.", "reasons": "An unnamed authority contrasts it with neglect."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p5", "position": "Success is continual worship and service without another deity.", "reasons": "Reported by al-Sulamī from an unnamed authority."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p6", "position": "Success is turning toward the Lord.", "reasons": "An unnamed authority contrasts this with turning away."}, {"id": "91:9/q12/p7", "position": "Purification restores the original fitra and perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes this as the successful person's attainment."}]}
{"id": "91:9/q13", "question": "How does this verse connect to nearby verses and the sūra's movement?", "turns_on": "Which adjacent sequence is emphasized: inspired choice, Thamūd, neighboring sūras, or broader scriptural parallels.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q13/p1", "position": "It turns inspired piety and vice into the opposed outcomes of moral choice.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī invokes 91:8 and 2:197: innate recognition makes submission natural and piety provisions lasting life. Corpus Coranicum sees opposing cosmic phenomena moving through morality in verses 7–8 to contrasting outcomes; Iṣlāḥī calls the soul a mirror of the world and a witness to accountability. Al-Ālūsī says the promise and threat attest to God's knowledge, necessary existence, perfect attributes and beneficence."}, {"id": "91:9/q13/p2", "position": "The success and failure contrast prepares and explains Thamūd's ruin.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says success follows piety in order and failure precedes Thamūd; if the pair answers the oath, Thamūd is evidence for the failed corrupter. Corpus Coranicum says the sūra does not explicitly state afterlife recompense, though 91:12 may imply it."}, {"id": "91:9/q13/p3", "position": "It links al-Shams to adjacent sūras' accounts of moral paths.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the previous sūra's right and left groups are summarized here and 91:8 explains the two paths in 90:10. Al-Biqāʿī says al-Layl continues divine power and divergent paths despite shared sensual aims, with night and sleep frustrating desires. Iṣlāḥī says al-Layl details the soul's corruption and protection."}, {"id": "91:9/q13/p4", "position": "Its blessing formula has Quranic and earlier scriptural parallels.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares Psalm 1:1 and especially 87:14, with related Quranic uses at 92:18, 80:3, 80:7, 79:18, 73:20 and 53:32. It says a pre-Islamic oath genre is repurposed with biblical creation ideas in verses 5–7."}, {"id": "91:9/q13/p5", "position": "The oath exhorts completion of the soul through knowledge and gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī calls knowledge of the Creator and gratitude the highest theoretical and practical excellences. Al-Rāzī says oaths by beneficial creatures prompt reflection and gratitude and weigh on hearts."}, {"id": "91:9/q13/p6", "position": "The pair became a central statement of purification teaching.", "reasons": "The Study Quran says it inspired extensive writing on purification, which some regard as the Quran's entire purpose."}]}
{"id": "91:9/q14", "question": "How is the divine-agent reading argued over?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb expresses actual divine causation, mere divine declaration, or an unacceptable attribution of evil to God.", "positions": [{"id": "91:9/q14/p1", "position": "God actually brings about purification, as the prayer asking Him to purify suggests.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites the prophetic prayer that God is the best purifier. Al-Rāzī rejects al-Qāḍī's weaker account of God merely judging or naming the soul pure: the verb form denotes bringing about, while divine judgment cannot change without truth becoming falsehood or knowledge ignorance."}, {"id": "91:9/q14/p2", "position": "Attributing purification and defilement to God wrongly assigns evil destiny to Him.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's attack on the divine-agent interpretation as Qadarite blame of God."}]}

{"id": "91:10/q01", "question": "What does repeating qad before the failure statement accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q01/p1", "position": "It confirms the certainty of failure and makes the oath apply to this assertion as well.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly gives both functions for the repeated particle."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q02", "question": "What does khāba say the loser has lost?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q02/p1", "position": "The person fails to attain the sought good or aim, ultimately lasting good and reward in the hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās glosses missing the goal; al-Qāmūs, quoted by Bursawī, adds loss and deprivation. Biqāʿī says the prepared afterlife reward is lost and effort is vain. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes durable benefit from immediate gain that ends in loss; Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise contrasts success in reaching a goal with failure. Elmalılı adds hopeless regret and cites 89:24. Corpus Coranicum observes that this sūra leaves afterlife recompense implicit, though 91:12 may suggest it."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q03", "question": "Who is the agent that buries or corrupts the soul?", "turns_on": "Whether the subject of the verbs resumes man or is God; grammatical pronominal return, the Prophetic prayer, transmitted glosses and the relation of human action to divine decree are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q03/p1", "position": "The human being acts upon his or her own soul.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ contrasts purification through obedience and charity with neglect. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ and others contrast obedience and good works with self-ruin through sin. Al-Zamakhsharī appeals to the surrounding inspiration and choice; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī say the apparent subject is man, with hā referring to the soul. Al-Naḥḥās finds a God-subject relative clause syntactically awkward; al-Samīn says the needed pronominal return through nafs and its possessor is awkward. Al-Ālūsī calls this the immediate reading while conceding the reports do not settle it. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats actor and soul as one being represented twice for choice and action; Jishumī finds the soul the natural antecedent."}, {"id": "91:10/q03/p2", "position": "God debases, hides, corrupts or misguides the soul, and the person thereby fails.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ikrima, al-Kalbī and others are transmitted for this reading. Al-Farrāʾ allows it. Al-Wāḥidī and Rāzī use the oath and prior decree to deny self-directed purification independent of God; Ṣāḥib al-Intiṣāf cites transmitted reports, consistent divine subjects in the oath, and parallel tazakkā. Ibn ʿAṭiyya invokes the Prophet's prayer to God as purifier. Al-Naḥḥās raises the relative-clause objection. Al-Zamakhsharī rejects this as attributing reprehensible destiny to God; al-Ālūsī says that charge is not established by the grammar or reports."}, {"id": "91:10/q03/p3", "position": "The wording permits human involvement under God's creating and decreeing of acts.", "reasons": "Bursawī says ordinary speech attributes a blow to Zayd although God creates the act; al-Rāghib distributes purification among servant, God, charity and worship. Al-Ālūsī says grammatical attribution requires human participation, not independent creation or power. Study Quran cites 35:18, 76:30, 4:49, 24:21 and 13:11 for the two sides. Qutb locates accountable choice within God's encompassing will and decree."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q04", "question": "What does the suffix hā refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q04/p1", "position": "It refers to the soul mentioned in verse 7.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls this the most plausible antecedent; al-Ālūsī pairs the suffix with a subject pronoun referring to man. Corpus Coranicum states the syntactic reference explicitly. Al-Samīn describes the return through nafs and its possessor as the difficulty for the God-subject analysis."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q05", "question": "What does dassāhā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word's concealment image is applied to sin, divine misguidance, specific moral states, hypocrisy or bodily matter; Corpus Coranicum disputes deriving the contextual sense from concealment.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q05/p1", "position": "To bury, hide, lower or diminish the soul through sin, neglect, ignorance or miserliness.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says the sinner hides and loses dignity; benefactors' conspicuous hilltop homes and fires versus misers' recesses illustrate the image, also developed by al-Muʿtazila, al-Qurṭubī, Biqāʿī and Ibn al-Jawzī. The unnamed poet praises visible hospitality; another line about ʿAmr illustrates burial or ruin. Al-Wāḥidī invokes 16:59 for concealment and says obedience is left unmanifest. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī contrast growth/elevation with diminishment. Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses prevention of good; al-Rāghib describes insertion of one thing into another. Elmalılı adds stunted virtue, vile bodily aims, ostentation and obscured divine light; Qutb speaks of weakening the conscious faculty. Ṭabāṭabāʾī likens the lost growth to a plant deformed by covert insertion."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p2", "position": "To misguide or seduce the soul into error.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported with closely related active and passive phrasings. Al-Qurṭubī cites a poem about ʿAmr's widowed wives; Durr's Ibn ʿAbbās survey glosses this term as leading astray. Some accounts assign misguidance to God, others to the person."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p3", "position": "To make the soul sinful, wicked, impure or corrupt.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives sin and wickedness; al-Lisān calls the term the antonym of zakā, impure. Corpus Coranicum prefers a separate poetic example for ruin/corruption to a sense derived only from Qurʾānic antithesis. Elmalılı links this to repeated deceit and spoiling. Biqāʿī specifies corrupt beliefs, acts, intentions and states."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p4", "position": "To ruin, destroy or lose the soul.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima glosses it as loss; al-Thaʿlabī transmits destruction from Ibn ʿAbbās; Ṭabrisī joins misleading and destroying. The cited poetry about ʿAmr supplies a concrete image of ruin and widowhood; the independent poetic usage is Corpus Coranicum's reason to prefer this sense."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p5", "position": "To deny the soul or call it false.", "reasons": "Two Ibn ʿAbbās reports in al-Ṭabarī give denial; al-Māwardī transmits denial or lying about the soul."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p6", "position": "To plot against or deceive the soul.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted with plotting, scheming or deceiving; Elmalılı also notes deceit and guile among the word's connotations."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p7", "position": "To conceal oneself among the righteous through ostentation without belonging to them.", "reasons": "Thaʿlab, Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Muʿtazilite interpreters supply this specific image; al-Qushayrī and al-Wāḥidī report it as an alternative."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p8", "position": "To make the soul wretched.", "reasons": "Ibn Sallām supplies this particular gloss."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p9", "position": "To turn the soul away from good.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk gives this gloss; Ibn ʿĀshūr similarly says preventing the soul from doing good."}, {"id": "91:10/q05/p10", "position": "To hide the soul in bodily matter and pollute it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports cleansing from material dross versus concealment in it; Qāshānī places the soul in the body's soil, away from divine light and mercy."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q06", "question": "How is the form dassāhā derived?", "turns_on": "Whether the contextual sense follows the doubled d-s-s concealment derivation or a contamination image; Corpus Coranicum says a hide/insert derivation makes little contextual sense.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q06/p1", "position": "It comes from the doubled d-s-s root, with one repeated sīn changed to a weak letter, normally yāʾ and then alif.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayda and the grammarians compare dassastu/dassasahā with qaṣaytu, taẓannaytu and taqaḍḍā; al-ʿAjjāj's hawk line and other poets illustrate substitution. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn describe replacement of the third repeated consonant; al-Ālūsī specifies yāʾ becoming alif after fatḥa and an intensified hiding sense. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes both dasā-yadsū and doubled dassā-yudassī. Al-Majāz gives mulibb from albabtu and a verse by al-Muḍarrib ibn Kaʿb for settled labīb. Elmalılı relates Turkish desise and the varied senses of desis and dessas to this root. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the substitution eases articulation."}, {"id": "91:10/q06/p2", "position": "Its contamination sense can be explained from wrapping or putting something into dirt, with an intensifying transformation.", "reasons": "Islāḥī gives this derivation, stressing the intensified sense of contamination."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q07", "question": "How does the verse relate human choice to God's decree?", "turns_on": "Whether the attribution to a human requires independent efficacy, whether divine misguidance may be attributed to God, and how the supplication and reported glosses bear on the subject.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q07/p1", "position": "People are responsible for the path they choose, while their capacity and acts remain within God's will and guidance.", "reasons": "Jishumī says God disclosed both paths and enabled both choices. Bursawī says God creates acts but they are attributed to their human performer. Al-Ālūsī denies that agency entails independent creation. Qutb joins freedom to accountability, divine measures in revelation and signs, and decree realized through conduct, citing 13:11. Study Quran combines human striving and God's will with 35:18, 76:30, 4:49, 24:21 and 13:11. Islāḥī likens heedlessness to closing one's eyes and falling; using divine gifts properly is gratitude, abusing them self-destruction."}, {"id": "91:10/q07/p2", "position": "The

 oath locates success and failure in God's prior purification, abandonment or misguidance, not independent self-purification.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, quoted by Rāzī, says the oath by noble creatures guards against supposing people independently reform or ruin themselves. Rāzī's school gives God the misguiding act. Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds support in the Prophet's supplication; al-Zamakhsharī attacks this attribution, while al-Ālūsī says its transmitted basis defeats his charge of Sunni inversion."}, {"id": "91:10/q07/p3", "position": "The human being's own purification or corruption determines the outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī sees the human action in the inspiration context and rejects the God-agent reading as attributing evil destiny to God. The reported Muʿtazilite glosses locate burial in the person's choices: immersion in sin, sinful company, neglected obedience or hiding among the righteous."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q08", "question": "What prayer is reported when the Prophet recited this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q08/p1", "position": "He asked God to grant his soul piety and purify it as its guardian and best purifier.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya connect the prayer to recitation. ʿĀʾisha says she heard it at night. Zayd ibn Arqam's longer report adds refuge from incapacity, laziness, miserliness, cowardice, senility or worry, grave punishment, useless knowledge, an unsated soul, an unhumble heart and unanswered supplication; the accounts vary in these additions. Ibn ʿAṭiyya uses the prayer to argue for God as purifier."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q09", "question": "How is the recitation of this sūra valued in a report?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q09/p1", "position": "A report likens reciting Sūrat al-Shams to giving charity to everything the sun and moon reach.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits the report through Ubayy ascribed to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q10", "question": "How are the verse endings pronounced in the reported readings?", "turns_on": "Degree of inclination of the final vowel and whether pronunciation follows the original form or ease of articulation.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q10/p1", "position": "Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim use fatḥ and tafkhīm.", "reasons": "Jishumī says fatḥ is the original pronunciation."}, {"id": "91:10/q10/p2", "position": "Al-Kisāʾī uses imāla throughout.", "reasons": "Jishumī explains imāla as easing pronunciation."}, {"id": "91:10/q10/p3", "position": "Other readers use intermediate or root-conditioned patterns.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the intermediate sound both eases pronunciation and indicates the original form."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q11", "question": "Do the success and failure statements answer the preceding oath?", "turns_on": "Whether a missing oath lām or an entire answer is supplied, and whether the statements are integral to the oath, parenthetical, or fronted.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q11/p1", "position": "Yes: the pair is the oath's answer or complement.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says most commentators take this view, with the lām of laqad omitted because the oath is long, and that it summarizes the sūra. Corpus Coranicum sees the eight-verse oath ending in opposed moral outcomes. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the pair the answer; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Sūrat al-Layl at 92:4–5. Al-Ālūsī argues omission of lām is common, especially after length, and lighter than omitting a whole clause; he invokes al-Zamakhsharī's treatment of 23:1 and says purification is a central goal."}, {"id": "91:10/q11/p2", "position": "No: they interrupt the oath, whose omitted answer threatens deniers with destruction like Thamūd.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī identifies Meccan deniers of Muḥammad and the parallel denial of Ṣāliḥ by Thamūd. Qāshānī elaborates that veiled deniers reject inspiration, let the dark self dominate and perish through transgression. Islāḥī endorses the suppressed-complement analysis but says omission lets the whole evidence of the oaths count; destruction of rebellious peoples is one prominent implication. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an interruption explaining divinely indicated piety. Al-Ālūsī counters that deleting the lām is easier than omitting a whole clause and denies that purification is a mere preliminary."}, {"id": "91:10/q11/p3", "position": "The oath's answer is omitted: 'you will surely be resurrected.'", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this alternative reconstruction."}, {"id": "91:10/q11/p4", "position": "The statements are advanced before the oath by inversion, without an omitted answer.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this word-order analysis."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q12", "question": "How does this failure statement connect to its surrounding verses and sūras?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is read chiefly as the culmination of the oath's contrasts, as a lesson embodied by Thamūd, or in relation to adjoining sūras; these links can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q12/p1", "position": "It completes a chain of contrasts between nature, moral capacity, purification and failure.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr lists sun/moon, day/night, disclosure/covering, heaven/earth, building/spreading, vice/piety and success/failure. Corpus Coranicum says the pre-Islamic oath genre is adapted with biblical creation ideas in verses 5–7, then proceeds to the moral pair. Abū Ḥayyān notes taqwā followed by success and failure followed by the next example, though the notes vary in describing that counterpoint. Elmalılı maps purification to daylight/sky and burial to night/earth. Jishumī says the signs reveal divine power and blessing."}, {"id": "91:10/q12/p2", "position": "Thamūd's coming denial and punishment exemplify the failure caused by corrupting the soul.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links 91:11 to arrogance and the failure claim; Abū Ḥayyān says God names a people after the general warning so others learn. Al-Zamakhsharī and Qāshānī read the parallel as the oath's suppressed threat to Meccan deniers."}, {"id": "91:10/q12/p3", "position": "It carries forward Sūrat al-Balad's two paths and anticipates al-Layl's account of moral divergence.", "reasons": "Jishumī says obedience here is called purification where the prior sūra called it the steep path. Biqāʿī says al-Balad's warning about rebellion at 90:11 spurs reform, while al-Layl explores differing paths despite shared desires; night's darkness and sleep, sibling of death, thwart aims. Al-Ālūsī links the previous right/left groups and 90:10's two paths to this summary. Islāḥī says al-Layl identifies corruption and protection of the soul. Study Quran also cites 90:10."}]}
{"id": "91:10/q13", "question": "What practical or spiritual lesson is drawn from the failure?", "turns_on": "The notes draw both a moral warning and an inference about divine attributes, without presenting them as mutually exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "91:10/q13/p1", "position": "Sin and neglect of obedience cause loss, so the verse warns people to cultivate piety, good works and vigilance.", "reasons": "Jishumī reads the pair as encouragement and warning; al-Rabīʿ connects good and evil acts to the two outcomes.
